1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Basic information: A 51-year-old female patient was admitted to the Department of Respiratory Medicine Ward 5, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University on Day 0, with the chief complaint of "chest tightness and shortness of breath after exertion for more than 3 years, worsened for more than 3 months." Three years earlier, the patient developed chest tightness and shortness of breath after exertion without an obvious trigger, accompanied by lip cyanosis, without dizziness, headache, or bilateral lower-extremity edema. She was treated symptomatically at a local hospital, with slight symptom relief. Three months earlier, the patient subjectively felt that the above symptoms had worsened and again presented to a local hospital. Chest CT showed: 1. thickening of the wall of the lower esophagus, with gastroscopy recommended for correlation; 2. inflammation in the bilateral lower lobes (Day -29). Upper abdominal + pelvic CT showed: 1. cirrhosis; 2. suspected esophageal and gastric fundal varices, with a cardia mass not excluded; please correlate with gastroscopy; 3. cholecystitis; 4. multiple small retroperitoneal lymph nodes; 5. thickening of the left adrenal gland; 6. absence of the uterus. Pulmonary artery CTA showed: 1. no obvious abnormality on pulmonary artery CTA; 2. inflammation in both lungs; 3. multiple small mediastinal lymph nodes; 4. thickening of the wall of the lower esophagus. Symptomatic treatment including antiasthmatic therapy was given, with no obvious improvement in symptoms. For further diagnosis and treatment, the patient presented to the emergency department of our hospital. Arterial blood gas analysis suggested: PO2 55mmHg, PCO2 23mmHg. Myocardial enzymes showed no abnormality. NT-proBNP: 59ng/L. Echocardiography: mild regurgitation of the mitral and tricuspid valves, mild aortic regurgitation, and reduced left ventricular diastolic function. She was admitted from the emergency department with the diagnosis of "chest tightness, cause to be determined." Past history: 28 years earlier, she received a blood transfusion locally due to cesarean section; 7 years earlier, she was diagnosed with hepatitis C and underwent splenectomy; 5 years earlier, she underwent hysterectomy for adenomyosis. Since the onset of this episode, the patient's appetite and sleep have both been normal; bowel movements and urination were normal; mental status was normal; and there was no weight loss. Previously, she had no history of hypertension or heart disease, no history of diabetes or cerebrovascular disease, no history of TB or malaria. Vaccination history followed the routine social immunization program. No history of trauma, and no history of food or drug allergy. Personal history, marital history, menstrual and reproductive history, and family history were unremarkable. Physical examination: The patient's general vital signs were stable. On examination: normal development, well-proportioned build, clear consciousness, fair general condition, chronic liver disease facies. Respiratory movement was normal, intercostal spaces were normal, tactile fremitus was normal, no pleural friction fremitus, no subcutaneous crepitus, percussion was resonant, breath sounds in both lungs were clear, with no dry or wet rales, and no pleural friction rub. No obvious abnormalities were found on abdominal, neurologic, or other examinations. Laboratory tests: Arterial blood gas analysis: pH 7.438↑, PCO2 29.60↓mmHg, PO2 66.5↓mmHg, total hemoglobin 142.00↓g/L, hematocrit 43.7↓%, oxygen saturation 93.90↓%. Complete blood count: white blood cell count 6.99×10^9/L, red blood cell count 4.5×10^12/L, hemoglobin 149.0g/L, platelet count 169×10^9/L. Coagulation tests: prothrombin time 15.90↑s, prothrombin activity 59.00↓%, activated partial thromboplastin time 35.6s, D-dimer 0.08mg/L. Blood biochemistry: potassium 3.33↓mmol/L, ALT 20 U/L, AST 37 U/L, albumin 29.8g/L, globulin 43.2↑g/L, direct bilirubin 10.3↑ μmol/L, indirect bilirubin 6.3μmol/L, CK-MB 46.0↑U/L. BNP precursor 30.4 pg/mL. Four-item infectious disease panel: hepatitis B virus e antibody 0.677 positive (+)↑COI, hepatitis B virus core antibody 0.0706 positive (+)↑COI, hepatitis C virus antibody 52.5 positive (+)↑COI, and the remaining indicators were negative. High-sensitivity hepatitis C viral load: target not detected. Urinalysis: occult blood 3+, red blood cells 25/uL, with no abnormalities in the remaining indicators. Stool routine, 3 inflammation markers, and glycated hemoglobin showed no obvious abnormalities. Pathogen-related indicators: 2 of 3 sputum cultures were positive (both Klebsiella pneumoniae, moderate amount). Fungal D-glucan 129.71 ↑pg/mL; human galactomannan was not elevated. Immune-related indicators: ANCA 4-item panel + comprehensive connective tissue disease panel: ANA (IgG type): 1:100 (±) (nuclear granular + nucleolar pattern), anti-Ro52 antibody qualitatively weak positive, quantitatively negative, and the remaining indicators negative. Autoimmune liver disease panel: ANA (IgG type): 1:100 (±) (nucleocytoplasmic granular pattern), and the remaining indicators negative. Rheumatoid arthritis panel: all negative. M proteinemia evaluation: no abnormal monoclonal immunoglobulin band detected. Immunoglobulins and complement: IgG 21.8 ↑g/L, complement C3 0.83↓g/L, complement C4 0.08↓g/L. ECG: ECG within normal range. Ultrasound: Heart: mild regurgitation of the mitral and tricuspid valves, mild aortic regurgitation, and reduced left ventricular diastolic function (emergency department). Reduced left ventricular diastolic function (repeat after admission). Liver/gallbladder/spleen/pancreas: status post splenectomy, diffuse echogenic changes in the liver, thickened and rough gallbladder wall; thyroid and cervical lymph nodes: bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy; urinary system: enlarged bilateral kidneys; veins of both lower extremities: no abnormality detected. Emergency CT report: Chest CT in the emergency department showed coarsened bilateral lung markings. Bilateral pleural thickening. Wall thickening of the lower esophagus and cardia; please correlate clinically. Case features: 1. young female, history of hepatitis C for more than 7 years, chronic liver disease facies; 2. recurrent dyspnea over the past 3 years; 3. laboratory tests: arterial blood gas suggested type I respiratory failure, D-dimer not elevated, indirect bilirubin elevated, reversed albumin/globulin ratio; 4. chest CT: no obvious acute pulmonary inflammation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hepatopulmonary syndrome
supporting_evidence: The patient has a definite background of chronic liver disease: hepatitis C was diagnosed 7 years ago; imaging suggested cirrhosis and esophagogastric varices; physical examination showed facies of chronic liver disease.

The main manifestations are recurrent chest tightness and shortness of breath on exertion for more than 3 years, accompanied by cyanosis of the lips, with recent worsening, consistent with manifestations related to chronic hypoxemia
Arterial blood gas indicates hypoxemia: PO2 55mmHg, oxygen partial pressure 66.5mmHg, oxygen saturation 93.90%↓, and decreased PCO2, suggesting hypoxemia with hyperventilation

Chest CT/pulmonary artery CTA showed no obvious pulmonary or pulmonary arterial abnormalities sufficient to explain the severe hypoxemia; the accompanying images show no obvious large areas of consolidation or diffuse interstitial abnormalities in either lung.
Cardiac enzymes showed no abnormalities, NT-proBNP 59 ng/L and 30.4 pg/mL, ECG was essentially normal, with insufficient evidence for cardiogenic hypoxemia
opposing_evidence: The phase 1 information did not provide clear contradictory evidence.

differential_diagnoses.name: Portopulmonary hypertension
supporting_evidence: The patient has evidence of cirrhosis and portal hypertension: imaging suggests cirrhosis and esophageal and gastric fundal varices.
Long-term progressive exertional chest tightness and dyspnea accompanied by hypoxemia may be seen in pulmonary vascular disease

No obvious abnormalities on pulmonary artery CTA do not exclude pulmonary hypertension, and the attached chest CT images show no obvious parenchymal lung disease, suggesting that a pulmonary vascular cause should be considered.

A non-elevated D-dimer and no abnormalities on venous ultrasound of both lower extremities provide insufficient evidence for a common venous thrombotic source, indirectly supporting the need to consider nonthrombotic pulmonary vascular disease
opposing_evidence: Emergency and follow-up echocardiography showed only mild mitral, tricuspid, and aortic regurgitation and impaired left ventricular diastolic function; in the first stage, no evidence of pulmonary hypertension or right heart enlargement was reported.
NT-proBNP is not elevated, not supporting a significant increase in right heart load

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic pulmonary embolism/chronic thromboembolic pulmonary vascular disease
supporting_evidence: The patient has had progressive exertional dyspnea and hypoxemia for more than 3 years, and chronic pulmonary vascular obstructive disease should be included in the differential diagnosis.
Cyanosis of the lips and type I respiratory failure may be seen in pulmonary vascular bed involvement
No obvious parenchymal lung lesions explaining the hypoxemia were seen on the accompanying chest CT images or in the report text.
opposing_evidence: Pulmonary artery CTA showed no obvious abnormality.
D-dimer 0.08 mg/L, venous ultrasound of both lower extremities showed no abnormalities
No acute chest pain, hemoptysis, or definite history of venous thrombosis was provided in the past history or in the first-stage information of this episode.

differential_diagnoses.name: Occult diffuse parenchymal lung disease or connective tissue disease-related pulmonary involvement
supporting_evidence: The patient has long-standing exertional dyspnea and hypoxemia; early or mild diffuse parenchymal lung disease should be considered.
Immune-related tests showed some abnormalities: ANA 1:100 (±), anti-Ro52 antibody weakly positive, elevated IgG, and decreased complement C3/C4, suggesting an underlying immune abnormality.

The chest CT report indicates coarsened bilateral pulmonary markings and bilateral pleural thickening; the accompanying images show mildly increased pulmonary markings, but no obvious lobar lesions are seen.
opposing_evidence: On lung examination, breath sounds were clear bilaterally, with no dry or moist rales.
Chest CT and the accompanying images did not show definite typical imaging features of interstitial lung disease, such as diffuse ground-glass opacities, reticular opacities, or honeycombing.

Most indicators in the connective tissue disease panel and rheumatoid arthritis panel were negative, and in the first stage no typical systemic manifestations such as rash, arthralgia, or dry mouth and dry eyes were provided.

differential_diagnoses.name: Cardiogenic dyspnea (mainly related to diastolic dysfunction or mild valvular regurgitation)
supporting_evidence: Echocardiography showed decreased left ventricular diastolic function, with mild mitral, tricuspid, and aortic regurgitation.
Clinically, there is chest tightness and shortness of breath on exertion
opposing_evidence: Both NT-proBNP 59 ng/L and 30.4 pg/mL are not elevated
The electrocardiogram was within normal limits, and cardiac enzymes showed no abnormalities.
During the first stage, no signs of heart failure were observed, such as bilateral lower extremity edema or pulmonary moist rales.
Marked hypoxemia, while the cardiac evaluation showed only mild abnormalities, insufficient in severity to fully explain type I respiratory failure

differential_diagnoses.name: Hepatopulmonary syndrome
evidence: The patient has a history of liver disease. Primary liver disease can cause intrapulmonary vascular dilatation and impaired arterial oxygenation, constituting the so-called triad. Clinically, it is characterized by primary liver disease and pulmonary abnormalities; characteristic manifestations are platypnea, hypoxemia, and cyanosis.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Right heart contrast echocardiography: After injection of a right heart contrast agent via the median cubital vein, dense contrast echoes were seen in the right atrium and right ventricle. At rest, after 3-5 cardiac cycles, the left heart was filled with contrast echoes, >30/frame. Ultrasound impression: Right heart contrast echocardiography: right heart contrast study (+) (consider intrapulmonary shunt).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has chronic liver disease and portal hypertension in the setting of hepatitis C, imaging findings suggestive of cirrhosis, and esophageal and gastric fundal varices. For more than 3 years, the patient has had recurrent chest tightness and shortness of breath after activity, accompanied by cyanosis of the lips, with worsening over the past 3 months. Arterial blood gas testing on multiple occasions indicated hypoxemia/type I respiratory failure, while chest CT, pulmonary artery CTA, ECG, NT-proBNP, and echocardiography did not reveal any significant pulmonary parenchymal lesion, pulmonary embolism, or cardiogenic cause sufficient to explain the hypoxemia. Repeat image review suggested increased vascular markings in the bilateral lower lungs, with possible pulmonary vascular dilation; hepatopulmonary syndrome should be a key clinical consideration. The purpose of contrast-enhanced transthoracic echocardiography is to directly determine whether there is a right-to-left shunt caused by intrapulmonary vascular dilation and to distinguish it from a simple intracardiac shunt; a result showing opacification of the left heart delayed by 3-5 cardiac cycles helps support intrapulmonary shunting as this key pathophysiologic mechanism, thereby providing core evidence for the diagnosis of hepatopulmonary syndrome, while excluding other differential diagnoses causing hypoxemia, and providing a basis for subsequent treatment decisions such as further evaluation of indications for liver transplantation.

recommended_exams.exam: Blood gas analysis in the standing and supine positions
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: To further clarify the diagnosis, upright and supine blood gas analyses were further completed. In the supine position, both the patient’s pulse oxygen saturation and blood gas analysis indicated increased oxygenation compared with the upright position, and the patient’s dyspnea was less severe in the supine position than in the upright position.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: This patient has long-term progressive exertional dyspnea, cyanosis, and definite hypoxemia. In the setting of chronic liver disease, hepatopulmonary syndrome is already highly suspected, but resting arterial blood gas alone cannot demonstrate its characteristic posture-related worsening of oxygenation. Obtaining arterial blood gas analysis in both the upright and supine positions is intended to objectively compare PaO2 and oxygenation changes under different postures and determine whether orthodeoxia with improvement in the supine position is present, that is, the orthodeoxia/platypnea commonly seen in hepatopulmonary syndrome. Because the patient's chest imaging showed no obvious acute inflammation or diffuse parenchymal disease, pulmonary artery CTA showed no abnormality, and cardiac evaluation also lacked supporting findings, this examination can further determine whether the hypoxemia is consistent with posture-related intrapulmonary shunting, thereby increasing diagnostic confidence for hepatopulmonary syndrome and reducing misclassification as other causes such as infection, heart failure, and pulmonary embolism; at the same time, it can also assess the severity of hypoxemia and provide a quantitative basis for oxygen therapy, periprocedural risk assessment, and subsequent treatment plan selection.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: In the supine position, both pulse oxygen saturation and arterial blood gas analysis indicated that oxygenation increased compared with the upright position, and the patient's dyspnea was less severe in the supine position than in the upright position.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient’s current main problem is recurrent and progressively worsening hypoxia-related dyspnea. Prior arterial blood gas testing has already confirmed hypoxemia, but the condition has a clear positional-change pattern. Pulse oximetry is noninvasive and allows continuous dynamic monitoring, making it suitable for repeated observation of changes in oxygen saturation in the upright and supine positions and at rest and during activity, for rapid detection of positional oxygenation decline and correlation with the patient’s subjective changes in dyspnea. In the context of this case’s chronic liver disease background, pulmonary and cardiac examinations being insufficient to explain the hypoxemia, and chest CT suggesting possible pulmonary vascular dilatation, dynamic pulse oximetry can help support the clinical features of hepatopulmonary syndrome and indicate whether there is upright-position worsening of oxygenation consistent with intrapulmonary shunting; at the same time, it can also be used to assess the severity of hypoxemia, monitor disease-course fluctuations, guide oxygen therapy and activity management, and serve as a safety monitoring method before and after further invasive or complex examinations.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Right-sided contrast echocardiography: After injection of a right-sided echocardiographic contrast agent via the median cubital vein, dense contrast echoes were seen in the right atrium and right ventricle. At rest, the left heart became filled with contrast echoes after 3-5 cardiac cycles, >30/frame. Ultrasound suggested: right-sided contrast echocardiography: right heart contrast (+) (consider intrapulmonary shunt). To further clarify the diagnosis, upright and supine blood gas analysis was further completed. In the supine position, both pulse oxygen saturation and blood gas analysis indicated increased oxygenation compared with the upright position, and the patient's dyspnea was less severe in the supine position than in the upright position.
